 Severe liver damage due to dengue fever.
 Two female patients, aged 23 and 53, were transferred to the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases with severe dengue fever. Both had severely low platelet counts, elevated liver enzymes of nearly 2,000 U/L, along with coagulation disorders and signs of organ damage. Notably, the disease can worsen even when the patient's fever begins to subside.
 Báo Pháp Luật Việt Nam • 11/11/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e Add Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e 0 Patient BH (53 years old, Hai Phong ) was previously healthy and had never had dengue fever. Approximately 5 days before hospitalization, she experienced a persistent high fever, sometimes reaching 39–40°C, accompanied by general body aches, nausea, frequent vomiting, and abdominal pain.
 The patient self-medicated with paracetamol at home, but their condition did not improve. Upon arriving at a medical facility, tests confirmed a Dengue virus infection, and a rapid decrease in platelet count from 38 to 21 G/L was observed. Liver enzymes were also elevated. Due to the complicated situation, the patient was transferred to the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases.
 At the hospital, the patient still had a high fever, severe pain in the right lower rib area, and petechiae (small hemorrhagic spots) appeared under the skin at the injection site. Tests showed platelet count was only 23 G/L, AST was elevated to 1,939 U/L, ALT was 804 U/L, along with coagulation disorders.
 Patients diagnosed with severe dengue hemorrhagic fever, liver damage, and coagulation disorders require close monitoring for the risk of bleeding, circulatory disturbances, and other complications.
 Another case involves a 23-year-old female patient, PL, from Hanoi , who was previously healthy. Approximately 7 days before being transferred to the hospital, the patient developed intermittent high fever, sometimes reaching 39°C, accompanied by chills, headache, body aches, abdominal pain, nausea, frequent vomiting, and loose stools.
 Following previous treatment at a medical facility, the patient's condition did not improve, and laboratory test results continued to deteriorate. Platelets decreased to 21 G/L; AST increased to 1,907 U/L and ALT to 883 U/L.
 Notably, the ultrasound results revealed fluid in the abdominal cavity and bilateral pleural spaces. This could be indicative of plasma leakage – a crucial mechanism in severe dengue hemorrhagic fever, which can lead to decreased circulating volume, hemodynamic instability, and shock if not detected and treated promptly.
 Upon transfer to the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases, the patient still had a fever, was very tired, had petechiae (small hemorrhagic spots) under the skin, and experienced pain in the liver area. Doctors assessed this as a severe case of Dengue hemorrhagic fever with serious liver damage, requiring close monitoring and intensive treatment.
 You may also like Just because the fever has subsided doesn't mean the illness is out of danger. 
 Currently, the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases is treating 16 patients with dengue fever, including some severe cases requiring close monitoring and intensive treatment.
 According to Dr. Pham Van Phuc, Deputy Director of the Intensive Care Unit at the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases, dengue fever is an infectious disease caused by the dengue virus, primarily transmitted through Aedes mosquitoes. The disease can occur at all ages, including those who were previously completely healthy.
 According to Dr. Phuc, thrombocytopenia (low platelet count) is a common symptom in dengue fever patients, but the severity of the disease cannot be assessed solely based on platelet count. The risk of complications needs to be evaluated holistically based on clinical condition and many other indicators such as signs of bleeding, blood pressure, pulse, urine output, blood concentration, and signs of organ damage.
 "In these two cases, in addition to a sharp drop in platelets, the patients also had very high liver enzymes, blood clotting disorders, and other warning signs. These abnormalities indicate that the disease has progressed seriously and requires close monitoring to detect and treat complications promptly," Dr. Phuc said.
 In particular, one of the key points to note about dengue fever is that the disease can worsen when the patient's fever begins to subside. The dangerous phase usually occurs between the 3rd and 7th day of the illness, when the patient may experience plasma leakage, severe bleeding, or organ damage.
 If not detected and treated promptly, severe plasma leakage can lead to hypovolemia, shock, multiple organ failure, and be life-threatening.
 Dr. Phuc emphasized that patients and their families should not assess the severity of the illness based solely on body temperature. A reduction in fever does not necessarily mean the illness has passed the critical stage.
 People who have or suspect they have dengue fever should go to a medical facility immediately if they experience warning signs such as severe or persistent abdominal pain, frequent vomiting, lethargy or restlessness, nosebleeds, bleeding gums, decreased urination, cold hands and feet, or extreme fatigue.
 You may also like If a doctor instructs the patient to monitor and treat the condition at home, the patient should rest, stay adequately hydrated, monitor their temperature, appetite, urine output, and any unusual symptoms. Do not increase the dosage of fever-reducing medication or use anti-inflammatory drugs without a doctor's prescription, as some medications can increase the risk of bleeding in dengue fever.
 Attending scheduled follow-up appointments, undergoing prescribed tests, and closely monitoring the patient during the 3rd to 7th day are crucial for early detection of the risk of worsening condition. Patients should not be complacent when their fever subsides or symptoms seem to improve, as this could be the time when the disease enters a dangerous stage.
 To proactively prevent dengue fever, people need to implement several measures simultaneously, such as eliminating stagnant water sources, destroying mosquito larvae, limiting mosquito bites, and maintaining a clean living environment. In addition, dengue vaccination is a proactive preventive measure that people can choose according to the instructions of healthcare workers and the regulations of vaccination centers.
 However, vaccination does not replace mosquito control measures and prevention of mosquito bites. If dengue fever symptoms are suspected, people should still go to a medical facility for examination, testing, and appropriate monitoring guidance.
 Dengue fever can be severe at any age. Early recognition of warning signs, especially between the 3rd and 7th day, following proper monitoring guidelines, and seeking timely medical attention are crucial factors in limiting complications and protecting the health and lives of patients. Proactive prevention, combining mosquito control measures with appropriate vaccination, will contribute to reducing the risk of contracting and experiencing severe dengue fever.
